dehydrated_text:
You do this because everyone wants to go to the Ivy League. But if you're an average school, you're just trying to recruit students. So, admissions officers at elite schools think like this: they want to admit students who will bring prestige to the university. Most other schools are focused on getting tuition payments.

So, why did Yale pick you? I'll explain later. Okay.

Harvard is essentially a venture capital firm. If you were a venture capitalist and had two options—Option One: someone wants to open a restaurant and needs $1 million. His uncle works in the government, so he guarantees that his restaurant will be frequented daily, ensuring at least $500,000 per year with no risk. Option Two: someone wants to start an AI and Bitcoin website but has no experience coding and an undefined idea. If successful, it could make a billion dollars.

You'd always pick Option One because low-risk ventures are less exciting than high-risk ones that might yield huge returns. This is Harvard's mentality; they want students who can change the world, not just solid performers.

Another saying: Harvard prefers having 10 people succeed and 999 fail rather than a thousand succeed slightly. We remember those who succeed and forget the rest. That’s why they're famous for creating brand recognition.

For my application to Yale, I went to a public high school in Canada, top 10 out of 200 students, but not the best. My SAT score was 1400 out of 1600, decent but not great. I played soccer and was captain of a quiz team called Reach for the Top. In my essay about Richard Feynman, it was boring and could have been written by anyone.

This is how they perceive your application: first, what you say; second, your background; third, your potential.
